digest.top_line: SPIRIT (Bhasin RCT): 12wk TRT in hypogonadal men post-RP for Gleason 3+3/3+4 → sexual activity +0.91 vs placebo (0.56-1.26, P<.001), zero biochemical recurrences either arm.
digest.tldr: Only readout today is a prostate survivorship study. Phase 2 SPIRIT supports short-course TRT for symptomatic hypogonadism after RP in low-risk men with PSA undetectable ≥2 yr. Sexual activity, desire and lean mass improved, but erectile function and energy did not. Zero BCR tells us little after 12wk exposure, since near-zero events were expected in either arm.

sites.intro: Prior RT and ADT were excluded, so these results don't carry over to hypogonadism after RT or salvage RT.

studies.name: Testosterone Treatment in Prostate Cancer Survivors (Bhasin RCT)
studies.tldr: Sexual activity +0.91 daily events vs placebo (95% CI 0.56-1.26, P<.001), zero biochemical recurrences, 12wk TRT in hypogonadal men post-RP for Gleason 3+3/3+4.
details: 🔍 SPIRIT: randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind phase 2, 2 academic centers, N=136 (68 vs 68)
💊 Testosterone cypionate 100 mg IM weekly × 12 wk vs placebo; stratified by site, age, PDE5I use

subdetails: Age ≥40, RP for organ-confined pT2N0M0, Gleason 3+3 or 3+4, preop PSA <10
Mean of 2 AM testosterone <275 ng/dL and/or free T ≤70 pg/mL
Plus low libido, ED, or fatigue

details.text: 📊 Treatment effect vs placebo (MMRM, weeks 6 and 12)

details: 📊 Lean mass gain: whole-body 2.56 kg (1.88-3.24), appendicular 1.50 kg, trunk 1.06 kg
📐 Effect 0.91 exceeds stated PDQ-4 MCID of 0.5 units
⚠️ 12 wk treatment + 3-mo f/u: cannot address clinical recurrence or long-term safety
⚠️ Low-risk cohort (undetectable PSA ≥2 yr) means expected BCR events near zero regardless of arm
⚠️ No multiplicity adjustment across secondaries; systemic T effects may compromise blinding of PROs

verdict.rationale: Efficacy primary met in a clean double-blind RCT, but the question that gates practice (oncologic safety) is untestable at N=136 and 12 wk; authors frame it as proof-of-concept.
verdict.audience: Hypogonadal men post-RP, pT2 Gleason 3+3/3+4, undetectable PSA ≥2 yr

studies.significance: Men treated with RT or ADT were excluded, so the zero-BCR signal does not transfer to post-RT survivors, the hypogonadal population a radiation oncologist actually follows. Post-RT pts retain prostate tissue, and this trial offers no data on TRT against that background.
studies.monday_clinic: In hypogonadal men with undetectable PSA ≥2 years after RP for pT2 Gleason 3+3 or 3+4 disease, this supports short-term TRT as an evidence-backed option for sexual symptoms; it does not extend to post-RT, post-ADT, or higher-grade survivors.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group phase 2** (SPIRIT), 2 academic centers, 1:1, N=136. Enrollment May 2019 to last visit May 2025; target revised from 142 to 134 with DSMB concurrence.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men ≥40 post-RP for **organ-confined pT2N0M0, Gleason 3+3 or 3+4**, preop PSA <10, **undetectable PSA ≥2 yr**. Hypogonadal (T <275 ng/dL and/or free T ≤70 pg/mL) plus low libido, ED, or fatigue. Mean age 68.6; 38% Gleason 6, 62% Gleason 7.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **Testosterone cypionate 100 mg IM weekly × 12 wk** vs placebo. Total T rose 349 ng/dL (95% CI 283-415) more than placebo; adherence 95% vs 94%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary efficacy:** change in sexual activity (PDQ question 4). **Primary safety:** biochemical recurrence (≥2 consecutive PSA ≥0.2 ng/mL). Secondary: desire, erectile function, affect, body composition, VO2 peak, stair-climb power.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No biochemical recurrence in either arm.** Erythrocytosis in 3 TRT pts; SAEs 1 vs 3; no MACE or VTE. One TRT pt had detectable PSA 0.1 to <0.2 ng/mL during treatment.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Described by the authors as the first randomized placebo-controlled trial of TRT in prostate cancer survivors; prior support for TRT after RP rested on observational series. Many guidelines still list prostate cancer history as a TRT contraindication.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents hypogonadal men with low-grade pT2 disease and durably undetectable PSA after RP. Does not represent men treated with RT or ADT, or those with high-grade disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Baseline recurrence risk in this cohort is so low that **0 vs 0 BCR carries little information** about harm. Erectile function did not move despite EPIC-26 gains, and no P value adjustment was made across secondaries.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The efficacy case for TRT in this population is now randomized and exceeds the MCID. The safety case remains a short-horizon absence of events, which justifies a larger long-term trial rather than settling the contraindication.

studies.interpretation:
The trial answers the question it could answer and is candid about the one it could not. On efficacy, the result is clean: a double-blind, placebo-controlled design with concealed randomization, an adjusted between-group difference in sexual activity of 0.91 daily events against a prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 0.5, and consistent movement in desire, the EPIC-26 sexual domain, negative affect, and lean mass. None of that is surprising; testosterone does these things in hypogonadal men generally. What is new is that it has now been shown under randomization in men with a prostate cancer history, which removes one argument guidelines have leaned on, namely that no randomized evidence exists.

The safety readout needs a more careful reading. Zero biochemical recurrences in both arms sounds reassuring, but the eligibility criteria selected men whose baseline recurrence risk over a six-month window was already close to nil: pT2N0M0, Gleason 3+3 or 3+4, preoperative PSA under 10, and PSA undetectable for at least two years. In that population one would expect no events whether testosterone promotes regrowth or not. The absence of recurrence here is compatible with safety but cannot discriminate it from modest harm. The PSA kinetics are marginally more informative: one TRT participant drifted to the 0.1 to under 0.2 ng/mL band, which is the kind of signal a longer trial would need to track, not dismiss.

The erectile function null is worth noting. EPIC-26 sexual domain improved while IIEF erectile function did not differ between arms, which fits a post-prostatectomy population in which erections are limited by nerve and vascular injury rather than androgen deficiency. Testosterone appears to act on desire and activity, not on the mechanical deficit, and clinicians should set expectations accordingly.

Blinding deserves some skepticism. Testosterone produces perceptible physiologic effects, and erythrocytosis occurred only in the treated arm; participants may have inferred allocation, and every sexual and affective outcome here is patient-reported. Secondary endpoints were not adjusted for multiplicity. Neither concern threatens the primary result much given its magnitude and the objective lean mass changes, but they temper confidence in the softer secondaries.

For radiation oncologists the boundary is the finding. Men treated with RT or ADT were excluded, so the trial says nothing about the irradiated prostate, where residual glandular tissue, benign PSA production, and bounce complicate surveillance on androgen replacement. Extrapolating the zero-recurrence result to post-RT survivors would import reassurance from a population with no prostate and near-zero risk into one with both. The same limit applies to higher-grade disease. What the trial does establish is a design template and an effect size that make a larger, longer safety trial feasible, which the authors state was its purpose.

significance_by_specialty.surgonc: For the urologist following hypogonadal men after RP for pT2 Gleason 3+3/3+4 disease, this provides the first randomized efficacy data for TRT, with an effect above the stated MCID. It does not settle oncologic safety: 0 vs 0 BCR over 12 wk plus 3 mo in a near-zero-risk cohort cannot rule out harm.

papers.title: Testosterone Treatment in Prostate Cancer Survivors With Hypogonadism: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract:
IMPORTANCE: A majority of men with prostate cancer have low-grade cancer and an excellent prognosis after radical prostatectomy. Hypogonadism and associated symptoms impair quality of life in prostate cancer survivors. Many guidelines, citing a lack of randomized clinical trials showing safety and efficacy of testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), consider a history of prostate cancer a contraindication for TRT.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the short-term safety and efficacy of TRT in prostate cancer survivors with symptomatic hypogonadism.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 2 trial was conducted at 2 academic medical centers in men 40 years and older with organ-confined, low-grade prostate cancer (Gleason score of 6 [3 + 3] or 7 [3 + 4]). Participants had undetectable prostate-specific antigen (PSA) for at least 2 years after radical prostatectomy, a mean of 2 testosterone levels less than 275 ng/dL, and low libido, erectile dysfunction, or fatigue. Patients were allocated using concealed, block randomization, with stratification for age (40-60 years or >60 years) and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (PDE5I) use. The first participant was randomized on May 13, 2019, and the last study visit was completed on May 16, 2025.

INTERVENTION: Testosterone cypionate, 100 mg, or placebo intramuscularly weekly for 12 weeks.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The primary efficacy outcome was sexual activity. Secondary outcomes included sexual desire, erectile function, well-being, body composition, aerobic capacity, and physical function. The safety outcome was biochemical recurrence (PSA ≥ 0.2 ng/mL).

RESULTS: A total of 136 men were randomized, 68 to receive testosterone cypionate, 100 mg, and 68 to receive placebo, and 125 men completed the study. Groups were similar at baseline (mean [SD] age, 68.6 [6.5] years; 52 [38%] had a Gleason score of 6; and 84 [62%] had a Gleason score of 7). No participant in either group experienced biochemical recurrence. TRT significantly increased sexual activity more than placebo, adjusted for PDE5I use and age (between-group difference, 0.91 daily events [95% CI, 0.56-1.26]; P < .001). TRT increased sexual desire and prostate cancer quality-of-life sexual domain score, and decreased negative affect more than placebo. Erectile function did not change. TRT significantly improved body composition, loaded stair-climbing power, and peak aerobic performance (VO2 peak) compared with placebo.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this randomized clinical trial, TRT for 12 weeks in men treated with radical prostatectomy for low-grade prostate cancer significantly improved sexual activity, sexual desire, well-being, body composition, physical function, and aerobic performance compared to placebo without biochemical recurrence. The trial was neither long enough nor large enough to evaluate clinical recurrence or long-term safety; this proof-of-concept trial was essential for rationalizing a larger, long-term study. These findings do not apply to men with high-grade prostate cancer or those treated with androgen deprivation therapy or radiation therapy.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT03716739.
